newsitem.title: POLAND: Warsaw bourse slide seen losing momentum next week.
newsitem.headline: Warsaw bourse slide seen losing momentum next week.

text.p: The Warsaw bourse is seen halting its two-week slide next week as lower prices are expected to stir up some fresh demand, but analysts see political wranglings over next year's budget weighing on the overall market mood.

"The market should react to the falls, at least briefly," said Dariusz Szepieniec, an analyst at Bank Slaski brokerage, adding that a 10.5 percent fall from this year's October 9 peak should make some prices attractive.

But some analysts said investors might be concerned with the political situation after the lower house of parliament, in a surprise vote on Thursday, chose to cut next year taxes for lowest earners, jeopardising the government's 1997 budget plan.

"If the political risk has increased and if the economic risk has increased than this will knock the market further, ...but we still have to evaluate how severe the risk is," said Stephen Pettyfer, an analyst at Merrill Lynch in London.

The finance ministry estimated the new rates, if cleared by the Senate and the President, would cost the budget 2.5 billion zlotys ($885 million) in lost revenues, threatening the planned 2.8 percent budget deficit target.
The vote split the ruling leftist coalition but on Friday several party officials hinted the two co-ruling parties were likely to seek a compromise and that the original decision could be reinstated.
Analysts said that if the market extended falls, 13,300 points would be a strong support for the main WIG index, which fell 8.3 percent to 13,499.4 points from last week's close.

Some analysts said foreign investors could be taking profits before the end of the year after the bourse's 90-percent growth so far, but were unlikely to pull out completely because Poland's economic fundametals remained too attractive.
They also said some attractive primary issues such as Bank Ochrony Srodowiska (BOS) and rubber maker Stomil Sanok were drawing capital away from the bourse, which contributed to the recent falls.
Analysts said Monday's figure on food prices growth in the October 11-20 period was unlikely to move the market after the central bank firmly said there was no room for a rate cut in the near future.

The week's biggest loser Espebepe plunged 31.5 percent to 4.25 zlotys after its new chief executive said on Tuesday the construction firm faced bankruptcy if it failed to clinch a debt-cutting deal with its creditors.
WBK fell 17.8 percent to 16.2 zlotys and Rafako plunged 17.5 percent to 16 zlotys.
